explanations.answer: The entrance to the Tent of Meeting
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says to bring it "…to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting to present it as an offering to the LORD before His tabernacle…" (Leviticus 17:4). Not wherever you happen to be standing, not wherever it's convenient. One address, and it's on the paperwork.

Big mountain, big energy, but that's not the spot here. God says to bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, before His tabernacle (Leviticus 17:4). Nobody in this passage is told to go climbing with an ox. I bet the ox is relieved.

explanations.answer: The banks of the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: Nice scenery, friend, but the river isn't mentioned in these verses. God names the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, where the offering is presented before His tabernacle (Leviticus 17:4). That's the one place He points to.

Bloodguilt is the word, baker. God says, "…that man shall incur bloodguilt. He has shed blood and must be cut off from among his people." I think this one is heavy, so it's good to hear it plainly. It's the LORD's own wording, and He doesn't water it down.

Nobody's reaching for a wallet here, friend. God doesn't mention money. He says the man "…shall incur bloodguilt." and "…must be cut off from among his people." (Leviticus 17:4). A fine would be a much smaller sentence than what the text says.

I can see why a curse comes to mind, since it sounds like that kind of verse. But the word God uses is bloodguilt. The text says the man "…has shed blood and must be cut off from among his people." (Leviticus 17:4). Stick to the exact word, baker, because the exact word matters.

Yep, the open fields. God says the Israelites will bring "…the sacrifices they have been offering in the open fields." to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 17:5). The sacrifices were already happening. The place is what changes.

Rooftops? Friend, I've seen some bold bakers, but nobody hauls a sacrifice up a ladder for fun. The text says something else. It says they've been offering them "…in the open fields." (Leviticus 17:5). Feet on the ground for this one.

City gates sound official, I'll give you that. But God says the sacrifices were being offered "…in the open fields." (Leviticus 17:5). Then they're brought to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. The fields are the answer, baker.

That's the one, baker. God says the Israelites "…must no longer offer their sacrifices to the goat demons to which they have prostituted themselves." Then He adds that this "…will be a permanent statute for them for the generations to come." (Leviticus 17:7). Permanent, friend. That's not a suggestion taped to the fridge.

Baal, a false god Israel later served (Judges 2:11), is a real name in the Bible, but he isn't in this verse. Here God says they must no longer offer their sacrifices "…to the goat demons…" (Leviticus 17:7). Easy one to mix up, baker, since the names sit close together in people's minds.

Molech does show up in the Bible, later in Leviticus 18:21, but not in these verses. In this passage God says they must no longer offer their sacrifices "…to the goat demons…" (Leviticus 17:7). It's a real name, friend. It just belongs to a different verse.

True, baker. God says if anyone from the house of Israel "…or any foreigner living among them…" offers a burnt offering or a sacrifice but doesn't bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, "…that man must be cut off from his people." (Leviticus 17:8-9). God names both the Israelite and the foreigner living among them. There's no side door.

This one is actually true, friend, so don't let the foreigner part trip you up. God says "…any foreigner living among them…" is included, along with anyone from the house of Israel (Leviticus 17:8). If they don't bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, "…that man must be cut off from his people." (Leviticus 17:9). The LORD names both groups on purpose.

explanations.answer: The life of the flesh is in the blood
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. God says, "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar…" (Leviticus 17:11). He explains Himself here, and the reason is life. Hold onto that one.

explanations.answer: The sickness of the flesh is in the blood
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible guess, but it's not what God says. His words are, "For the life of the flesh is in the blood…" (Leviticus 17:11). Life, friend, not sickness. The text gives life as the reason.

explanations.answer: The curse of the ground is in the blood
explanations.explanation: That sounds dramatic, I'll give you that. But God's reason is simpler: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood…" (Leviticus 17:11). Nothing about a curse or about the ground there. Just life.

On the altar, baker. God says He has given the blood "…to make atonement for your souls upon the altar; for it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul." (Leviticus 17:11). He gave it for that purpose, and He says so Himself.
Doorposts are a good guess, friend, but they're not in this verse. God says He gave the blood "…to make atonement for your souls upon the altar…" (Leviticus 17:11). The altar is the place He names.
Foreheads would be a bold choice, baker. But the verse doesn't say that. God says the blood is given "…to make atonement for your souls upon the altar…" (Leviticus 17:11). Altar it is.

explanations.answer: Drain it and cover it with dirt
explanations.explanation: Out in the field, a hunter who catches a wild animal or bird that may be eaten "…must drain its blood and cover it with dirt." (Leviticus 17:13). That goes for an Israelite and for a foreigner living among them. Two steps, and God doesn't skip either one. I've followed recipes with less clear instructions than that, and mine had pictures!

explanations.answer: Pour it out on the altar
explanations.explanation: The altar is where the blood goes in the sacrifices, so I see the connection. But this verse is about a hunted wild animal or bird that may be eaten. For that, God says the hunter "…must drain its blood and cover it with dirt." (Leviticus 17:13). A hunter in the field is a different situation, friend.

Fire does come up in this passage, since the priest burns the fat (Leviticus 17:6). But here God says the hunter "…must drain its blood and cover it with dirt." (Leviticus 17:13). Dirt, baker, not fire. I'd keep the matches in the drawer on this one.

explanations.answer: Wash his clothes and bathe with water
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The person "…must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening; then he will be clean." (Leviticus 17:15). Both parts are required, the clothes and the bath. It covers someone native or foreign.

explanations.answer: Offer a lamb at the altar
explanations.explanation: A lamb is a big ask, and God doesn't ask for one here. This verse says the person "…must wash his clothes and bathe with water…" (Leviticus 17:15). Then he's unclean until evening, and after that he will be clean. Just the washing, friend.

explanations.answer: Stay outside the camp for a week
explanations.explanation: A whole week outside would be a long time to wait. But the text doesn't say that. The person must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and "…he will be unclean until evening; then he will be clean." (Leviticus 17:15). Evening, baker, not a week.

This one is false, friend. The text doesn't say seven days. God says the person "…must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening; then he will be clean." (Leviticus 17:15). Evening, and then clean. The seven days just aren't in this verse.

False is right, baker. Here's what the text says: he "…will be unclean until evening; then he will be clean." (Leviticus 17:15). It happens after he washes his clothes and bathes with water. No seven days anywhere in the verse.
